6.0.s.en: (1) Christ's preaching in His own country

6.0.0.en: "And he went out from thence": that is, from Capernaum, west of the sea and the river Jordan.

6.0.1.en: "And came into his own country": that is, Nazareth in the north, and it is the place where the Lord spent His childhood and youth until He began to preach.

6.1.0.en: "The sabbath day ... the synagogue": the Sabbath was the day of worship, and if a Jew was in Jerusalem he went to the temple, but in the other cities synagogues were spread about, and they are places set apart for worship, prayers, explanation and interpretation, without the offering of sacrifice, for the sacrifices have their place in the temple alone in Jerusalem. "When they heard": St. Mark pointed to the reaction of the people in being amazed at Christ's teaching, new in its concept and powerful in its effect, and also their wondering and asking about the secret of His wisdom and His miracles of healing.

6.1.1.en: "The carpenter, the son of Mary": a reference to the work that Christ did before the preaching, which is a simple work. They also mentioned His mother, and mentioned the sons of Mary the wife of Clopas, the sister of the Virgin, who were the sons of His maternal aunt, and Jewish custom considers the sons of a maternal aunt to be brothers.

6.1.2.en: "They were offended at him": that is, they differed over His person. And the cause of the offense was the earlier talk among the people about the person of Christ, for they knew His upbringing and His family, and wondered and scoffed at Him because of what was being spread about His fame and His works.

6.2.0.en: "A prophet is not without honour": the Lord used a proverb well known among the Jews, whose meaning is that a person may find honor, standing and welcome abroad more than he finds it among his relatives who despise him.

6.3.0.en: "He could there do no": ... "could not" does not mean the inability of Christ or any lack of His power, God forbid, and what is meant by it is that, because of their unbelief, they deprived themselves of the works of the Lord, except a few who obtained healing because of their faith in Him. But Christ did not despair of their ingratitude, but kept going about the places near Nazareth preaching in them. A counsel, beloved ... unbelief prevents and veils the work of God in our lives, and pride prevents the knowing of the humble God.

6.4.0.en: "By two and two": Solomon the Wise says: "Two are better than one ... for if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow" (Eccl 4:9, 10), and the wisdom of the Lord in this is that each of them should be a support to the other, especially since the disciples were in their first experiences of the work of preaching, and the Lord did not leave them without help, but gave them power over Satan and the casting out of unclean spirits.

6.5.0.en: The Lord Christ forbade His disciples some things, so that they would not be occupied with anything away from the work with which they were charged, and so that they would experience His divine provision for all they would need of material things during their service. "A staff only": it is the only thing that Christ permitted the disciples, a clear reference to the Cross, which is the strength of help for the servant who is sent.

6.5.1.en: "Scrip": the bag that a traveler carries to put his things in.

6.5.2.en: "Bread": that is, food ... for I am the One who will provide this for you.

6.5.4.en: "Neither put on two coats": that is, being content with little, and with what is absolutely necessary, for God provides the rest of their needs.

6.6.0.en: "There abide ... till ye depart": that is, not being occupied with moving about and with feasts in many houses, but being content with what is necessary, which is staying in one house and concentrating on proclaiming the gospel and serving only.

6.7.0.en: This verse makes clear the recompense for man's refusal to accept the word of God that is necessary for his salvation, for the punishment at the judgment, if the refusal continues, which means blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, will be more severe than God's punishment when He burned Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen 19:24).

6.7.1.en: "Shake off the dust": a well-known custom among the Jews, whose meaning is that these people are not worthy of association or of sharing in anything, not even the dust of their town. And it means that whoever rejects the servants of God rejects God, because the servant here is a representative and ambassador of Christ Himself.

6.8.0.en: The disciples began their work as Christ had commanded them, so they began with teaching and preaching the Kingdom, making clear that the way is repentance ... and God gave them power and gifts, so they were able to cast out demons, and likewise to heal the sick by prayer and anointing with oil.

6.8.1.en: "Anointed with oil": the anointing with oil became a sacrament and a tradition in the Church, received from the Fathers the Apostles (see Jas 5:14).

6.9.0.en: St. Mark speaks here of the reactions of the people and of Herod the king to the preaching of Christ, for some of the people said "That it is Elias," who had gone up to heaven, come down alive once again, and these are his wonders. And others said that He is a prophet by whom God visits His people after the sending of prophets had ceased for hundreds of years. As for Herod, his sense of guilt over the unjust killing of John the Baptist made him say that it is John, risen from the dead, and mighty works are shown in him, and perhaps he has come to take vengeance on me.

6.9.1.en: Beloved ... this feeling of Herod is the feeling of many of the wicked who sacrificed their peace of heart for the lust of sin ... for lust made him kill, and after that peace left him, for Isaiah says: "There is no peace, saith my God, to the wicked" (Isa 57:21). So do not be deceived, my friend, by sin, for its price is heavy on earth and heavier still in eternity.

6.10.0.en: St. Mark here explains the story of the killing of John the Baptist from the beginning, and the motives and events that surrounded it, for John, while teaching the crowds and preaching repentance, also rebuked Herod Antipas, the son of Herod the Great who killed the children of Bethlehem, because he had put his brother Philip in prison and taken his brother's wife as his own wife, which made Herod (the son) seize him and imprison him, to be rid of his rebuking.

6.11.0.en: Jealousy took hold of Herodias, and feelings of rage and anger toward John possessed her, and she wanted to kill him, but the one who prevented her was Herod himself, who, although he had seized him, feared him and respected him, and knew that he was a man of God. And he heard many of his sayings and kept them, and likewise all the works that he did...

6.11.1.en: And this is the spiritual awe that God puts on the faces of His children before their persecutors, who may possess weapons and authority, but inwardly fear them and respect them.

6.12.0.en: At a banquet that Herod held in remembrance of his birthday, to which he invited his lords (his ministers), high captains (the chiefs of his army) and chief estates of Galilee (its notables), Salome, the daughter of Herodias, came in and danced, and her dancing was a source of delight and praise for those present. And as exhilaration took hold of Herod, he wanted to reward her, so he spoke with the boasting and pride of the kings of the earth that she should ask whatever she would, even up to half of his kingdom, and he increased in folly when he made his promise to her with an oath, which made going back on it impossible.

6.12.1.en: Have you seen, my friend, to what drunkenness and lust and the pride of greatness lead?! Do they not lead to folly and impulsiveness and rashness, in which everything is lost, the most important being wisdom?

6.12.2.en: So take heed, my friend, and let nothing take from you your will, your awareness and your decision.

6.13.0.en: St. Mark points out here, as St. Matthew also pointed out (14:8), that what the daughter asked was nothing but the carrying out of her mother's wicked desire for vengeance on John, who represented, even in his prison, the voice of the conscience that does not sleep, which the wicked man always wants to silence, and for this reason she asked ... at once the head of John the Baptist on a charger, which adds cruelty and bloodthirstiness also to her character.

6.14.0.en: The king was sorry, and it was possible for him to go back on his word. But, because of his pride before his guests and what he had sworn, he went on in his error all the more, and sent the executioner to behead John. And this reminds us of Pilate, who, despite the warnings of God, feared for his position, and sent the innocent Christ to the Cross.

6.14.1.en: My beloved God ... so it is with the chain of evil once it begins, for it continues and grows more inflamed, and leads to what cannot be avoided, for the fire of evil devours everything even if its beginning was a small spark ... I beseech You, my God, keep me from evil and from myself and from my passions, for I am a weak man and I have none but You in whom to take refuge.

6.15.0.en: In a scene that shows the ferocity of the human soul possessed by evil, Salome the daughter took the severed head and went with it to her mother, to quench her thirst for revenge with this sight. But the faithful disciples of John took his body and prepared it with spices according to the custom of the Jews, and buried it in sorrow and honor.

6.16.s.en: (4) The return of the twelve and the feeding of the five thousand

6.16.0.en: After relating the story of the martyrdom of John the Baptist, St. Mark takes us back to his account of the sending out of the disciples and their return to Christ. It was natural that the first thing the Apostles did was to tell Christ all that they had done. But Christ, in His tenderness and concern for everything, was not distracted by the reports of the service from caring for the bodily and psychological condition of His disciples, so He called them to some rest after the weariness. And since they had forgotten to eat amid their occupations, He did not forget, so He called them to be alone with them away from the crowding of the crowd, and for this reason He took them to a ship, to a quieter place.

6.16.1.en: What Christ did with His disciples was most gentle and tender ... He cares for everything ... so what of me, who forget many tender feelings amid the crowding of life?! And perhaps this is what people needed from me more than anything else ... Teach me, my Lord, to be like You as far as I am able.

6.17.0.en: But the crowds who were always pursuing Christ saw Him going with His disciples, and ran there quickly, and others came out of the villages and cities and gathered where Christ was sitting with His disciples in the ship. And when Christ looked out from the ship, He saw the very large numbers and had compassion on them, for they were as sheep not having a shepherd, and He began to teach them with various teachings as He did in the Sermon on the Mount. And after a long preaching, many hours, His disciples came to Him, saying:

6.17.1.en: "This is a desert place": that is, the place is far from habitation and markets and places where food is sold, "and now the time is far passed": a reference to the length of time and the hunger of the crowds...

6.17.2.en: Then came the suggestion offered by the disciples to solve this problem, which was to send the crowds away so that they might buy what they lacked of food.

6.18.0.en: Christ's answer came as a surprise to the disciples: "Give ye them to eat"!! ... From where, You who know everything, for we do not have food for these ... and if You meant that we should go and buy, we need at least two hundred pennyworth for bread alone ... and this shows that the number was large. And of course the Apostles' question carried a measure of astonishment at Christ's words!! ... and this is an encounter that often happens between God's will and His all-embracing provision, and man's helplessness and his actual limited abilities...

6.19.0.en: "Go and see": of course Christ knew the number of the loaves and fishes, but He charged the disciples with this so that they might make sure for themselves that there was nothing but this small amount. And it seems that they called out to the crowd ... whoever has food, let him bring it, because St. John mentions that a lad brought it. And some hold that the five loaves point to the five books of Moses, and the two fishes to the Old and New Testaments.

6.19.1.en: Then He commanded the disciples to make the crowd sit down in groups, company by company, to make the distribution easier ... and the disciples did so, so there were groups of a hundred and others of fifty.

6.20.0.en: "He looked up to heaven": the Lord wants to teach us that in our need we have no help but our heavenly Father.

6.20.1.en: "Blessed": because He is God, the source of every blessing, and "brake" means that He is responsible for dividing the good things and the blessings among all His creation, and His Church especially.

6.20.2.en: "Gave them to his disciples": God respects the role of His servants, so He does the work that they cannot do, but they have their role in the labor, and then in rejoicing in the work of God, especially after everyone had eaten and was filled.

6.21.0.en: The crowd was great and the food was plentiful. And St. Matthew adds to St. Mark that: "They that had eaten were about five thousand men, beside women and children" (14:21). And what remained of the fragments was twelve baskets, corresponding to the number of the disciples, so that each one of them might be a witness to this miracle for himself, for St. John mentions (6:12) that it was Christ who charged the disciples with gathering the fragments.

6.21.2.en: (1) That this miracle is the only one that the four Gospels mentioned because of the fame it brought to the Lord Christ, for everyone of the crowd who ate became a preacher of it (Mt 14:15-21; Lk 9:

6.21.4.en: (2) Because of the importance of this miracle, the Church placed it in the readings of her Liturgies, and it is read on the fifth Sunday of the Coptic month, which is usually called "the Sunday of the Blessing."

6.21.5.en: (3) Among the loveliest spiritual meanings in this miracle is the offering of your few resources in the hand of Christ, even if only a few minutes in the day ... offer them faithfully, and let God bless them and multiply them, so that you are filled first ... and fill others, and then be a witness and servant of His.

6.21.6.en: (4) The gathering of the fragments teaches us not to be wasteful in the breaking of bread, for often we throw what is left over from us into the rubbish, while others may not find it.

6.22.0.en: "And straightway": that is, after the filling of the crowds, He commanded His disciples to take the boat and go toward Bethsaida. But He Himself waited to accomplish two things, which were: sending away the crowds with the tenderness of a father bidding farewell to his children. And the second thing was withdrawing by Himself for prayer, in a practical lesson to all servants that the service of the crowds should not draw them away from caring to be alone with God and speak with Him. For there is no work in the life of the faithful servant more splendid than standing and speaking with God, so that he casts all his problems on his Father, and thanks Him for His great works with him.

6.23.0.en: "When even was come": that is, the time of sunset, for the Jews had two evenings, the first being the time of the afternoon in which the miracle of the feeding took place, and the second the time of sunset. And St. Matthew mentioned both evenings in his account (14:15, 23), and Christ was standing on the shore, looking at the ship in the midst of the sea, which was raging greatly, so that the disciples were afraid and were making every effort at rowing for the saving of their lives.

6.23.1.en: "The fourth watch": that is, the last part of the night, roughly from three in the morning until the end of the dawn, and this indicates that Christ left them in a very long and hard struggle, and did not intervene except at the last moment. And this means that God may leave us for a time so that we strive against the currents (lusts and difficulties), for striving unto blood (Heb 12:4) is required of us ... for God loves us and He is the shepherd of our souls. But in His wisdom He knows when to leave us and when to hasten to rescue us ... for there is a difference between love and the pampering that spoils a man. "Walking": ... that is, He left the shore and walked on the water to rescue them. And from the darkness and fear, they thought that He had passed by the ship ... and could not make out His features, and thought Him a ghost or a phantom, so their fear increased to the point of crying out. "Would have passed by them": passing by here does not mean "leaving," but He intended to get a little ahead of them so that they might see Him.

6.24.0.en: The disturbance and fear increased with the psychological exhaustion of the struggle with the sea all night, and here came the words of Christ: "Be of good cheer: it is I; be not afraid." And when He went up into the ship, the wind ceased entirely, which greatly astonished the disciples.

6.24.1.en: So it is, beloved ... if Christ enters our lives, there is calm and rest and reassurance ... for there is no peace outside Christ, and no peace like the peace of Christ.

6.25.0.en: "They considered not the miracle of the loaves": that is, the cause of their wonder and fear was their failure to realize that the God who was able to fill the crowds from five loaves is Himself able to walk on the water. "Their heart was hardened": that is, it had not yet been lit with complete faith ... and this happens to us often in times of affliction, for we forget the earlier good works of God.

6.26.0.en: The ship crossed over to the land of Gennesaret (a plain on the western side of the sea south of Capernaum) and anchored there, and the people recognized Him when He came out of the ship, though it was early morning.

6.27.0.en: The people began to gather their sick, including the lame among them, to bring them to Christ to obtain healing. And every place Christ entered, He would heal their sick; and to show the large numbers of those who were healed, St. Mark mentions that as many as touched Him were made whole.

6.27.1.en: The clean and the unclean, the healing of the Canaanite woman's daughter, the healing of the deaf man with an impediment
